This research examines the discretized version of a distributed regulation issue featuring a random differential equation as the state dynamic component. By leveraging the results of a random analytic regulator theory, we establish the existence of a discrete solution for a suitable approximation of the original problem. We also consider a specific random diffusion model as a specific example.

Our research examined the size of cosmic-ray fluctuations detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory for particles exceeding 4 EeV in energy. To achieve this analysis, we grouped observed air showers by the orientation of their electric field, taking into account various corrections, and calculated the standard deviation of signal amplitudes for a specific detector array configuration. Our main finding revealed a significant increase in the standard deviation of signal amplitudes at larger shower sizes, which can be attributed to fluctuations in cosmic-ray interactions rather than local effects. By combining this result with existing data on cosmic-ray spectra, we determined the apparent depth of cosmic-ray generation, finding it to be 12.2 +/- 1.2 (stat) +/- 2.5 (sys) EeV with an electron equivalent charge of 55 +/- 6 (stat) +/- 5 (sys). This research also identified the most probable cosmic-ray particle type as either a strange quark or a charm quark, which we believe is a first in the study of cosmic rays.

This paper proves that any variation of Zinbiel algebras automatically becomes an abelian algebra when using the definition from [6, 2.1], although it appears this fact has been inadvertently proven in [2, Proposition 3.3].

This study provides the first detailed examination of Luminosity- and beam-gas nucleus (A) dependence of fluctuation measures, specifically for the thermal nature of particle distributions, using Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. Multiple fluctuation measures were examined, including centralized and non-central collisions, using both the ALICE Betti map and cumulative variance methods. The results show that the stream angle affects fluctuation measures more significantly than initial predictions, indicating that the particle distributions are thermally driven. Additionally, the findings indicate that the average flow intensity in non-central collisions is substantially higher than initial estimates, further suggesting a strong connection to particle-fluid interaction.

In our proposed method, we aim to rectify inaccuracies in data tables that contain both missing values and functional relationships between elements. Similar to existing approaches, our strategy involves comparing two versions of the same data: a pristine reference, against an imperfect target containing the missing information. Here, we distinguish our method from prior work by incorporating silent errors represented by missing entries in the target data. Unlike traditional methods that treat nulls as equivalent to incorrect entries, we view them as distinct, given the target's potential to perfectly match the reference with appropriate data filling. Our solution involves identifying areas in the target that require adjustment based on the existing data and its relationships, without assuming additional information beyond what is already provided. In contrast to insertion or deletion operations, we may need to replace existing data with new content, a process that requires additional caution to avoid introducing additional errors. By leveraging graph-based techniques, our method incorporates a critical inspection of the data's integrity after applying the corrections, ensuring consistency with the established functional relationships. Here, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to real-world datasets containing missing values and varying levels of functional dependencies, along with synthetic examples showcasing the method's performance under different scenarios of data quality.

This study presents a novel dynamic modeling approach for count-based time series,
building on the foundations of autoregressive models. Our new model, TVPAR, addresses
issues associated with stationary Poisson autoregressive models, which require the
parameter matrix to remain constant and result in overestimations of confidence
intervals. TVPAR models incorporate changes in the parameter matrix over time and
are estimated through quasi-maximum likelihood optimization. The new model also
includes tests for detecting parameter matrix variations, assessing their significance,
and incorporates a Bayesian approach for this purpose. Furthermore, TVPAR models
can be applied to forecast future time series values. The benefits of TVPAR are
demonstrated through comparative simulations, comparing it to static PAR models, and
real-world data applications.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
leverages both category-level and instance-specific information, enabling
robust object identification across different poses and locations. In traditional
frameworks, object representation methods are typically separated into two
distinct categories: those that focus on identifying specific instances (e.g.
point clouds or 2D images) and those that categorize objects based on physical
attributes (e.g. shapes, weights). However, in critical manipulation tasks, both
precision and physical understanding are necessary for successful protocol execution.
To address this challenge, we combine NDFs with physical modeling, demonstrating
improved performance in challenging scenarios such as object sorting, satellite manipulation, and assembly tasks. Furthermore, NDFs exhibit inherent insensitivity
to SE(3) transformations, eliminating the need for additional learning tools
and providing robust results in real-world applications. Our code is available at
https://github.com/vishalsharma/neural-descriptor-fields.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classical statistics. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to compare the performance of different optimization methods for minimizing a given function. This comparison often leverages the concavity of the function in question, particularly in its early stages. For a specific function of significant interest, the Nishimori function (also known as the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model or the TAP free energy), we have previously established its local concavity using the Atkin-Sah, Mézard, and Parisi (AMP-MEZ-PAR) framework. Building upon the basics of AMP-MEZ-PAR, we develop a novel argument to demonstrate the sustainability of the Sudakov-Fernique phenomenon, which in turn ensures the local concavity of the TAP free energy along the Nishimori edge. The Sudakov-Fernique phenomenon refers to the sharp decline of the average of a quadratic function's minimum value across random vectors. Our proof of the Sudakov-Fernique phenomenon relies on a random vector distribution characteristic of replica symmetry, which can be ensured by selecting a specific temperature or bias. The resulting inequality holds not only in the large $N$ limit but also in the finite $N$ regime, where it is 1/N-fold concave. The detection of extra-galactic planets and aerosol gratings from UV stellar spectra holds significant promise in assessing the clarity of distant stars. As future astronomical missions observe an immense number of stars simultaneously, the ability to analyze their clarity automatically will be crucial. This work discusses recent advancements in developing and evaluating machine learning-based techniques for detecting planetary systems and assessing the level of aerosol obstruction in extra-galactic stars using photometric data. It also explores recent discoveries made using these methods and discusses the potential of future experiments to study planetary systems and aerosol distributions in extra-galactic environments.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based software for Generalized Graphical Lasso
computation. Generalized Graphical Lasso extends the well-known Lasso regression
and Graphical Lasso estimation beyond continuous outcomes to account for outcomes
with binary, Poisson, or gamma distributions. Outcomes with these distributions often
require modeling through link functions and scale parameters, which can affect the
estimation. Generalized Graphical Lasso uses the inverse Wishart distribution to
initialize and update the Hyper Hyper Inverse Wishart (HH IW) sampler, a Markov
Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, to facilitate efficient estimation. We introduce
a new version of the HH IW sampler, enhance the HH IW sampler with a degree of
freedom update, and demonstrate the efficacy of Generalized Graphical Lasso for
binary, Poisson, and gamma outcomes.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been rigorously compared and evaluated, revealing that the Langevin dynamics method stands out due to its minimal computational cost, robustness, and effectiveness in maintaining simulation accuracy. As a result of its efficiency, Langevin dynamics finds widespread application in molecular dynamics simulations utilizing extensive molecular configurational space explorations. To maximize the benefits of Langevin dynamics, a new algorithm called DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Space Sampling with Harmonic reweighting) is introduced, which simultaneously manages the speed of simulation and ensures adequate coverage of the configurational space. By generating configurational distributions in the canonical ensemble through harmonic reweighting, DASH ensures that the inherent friction affects configurational distribution, thereby neglecting the impact of friction on subsequent analyses. Overall, the dynamic and adaptive characteristics of DASH enable users to set an a priori time frame, convert it into an equivalent temperature range, and obtain a pre-determined number of configurational samples at the end, further enhancing the scalability and effectiveness of the method.

Understanding the dynamics of complex networks relies heavily on analyzing significant nodes, especially in scenarios where critical information spreads quickly. In multi-layer networks, defined by separate layers representing distinct time points or categories, the significance of nodes is not constant and varies across each layer. There is no standardized approach to determining node significance, but it is often estimated using eigenvalue-based methods, such as the largest eigenvalue of a network's adjacency matrix and its corresponding eigenvector. With varying definitions of node significance, a universal framework is proposed to address several key issues, including uneven distribution of nodes, reference layers for comparing significance, and dynamic networks with time-varying layers. Furthermore, a proposed indicator, called the eigenvector prominence (EVP), leverages eigenvalue-based approaches to evaluate the prominence of nodes across each layer, offering a valuable tool for identifying pivotal nodes that drive network dynamics and influence the spread of information.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

This study utilized high-speed imaging to examine spheres interacting with a flowing liquid surface across various speed regimes, from stagnant to supersonic, with results focused on seal formation.  A key finding is that at moderate speeds, spheres can create a precise seal using surface tension, with the condition requiring a gentle approach and minimal disturbance.  Furthermore, at these speeds, surface tension enables spheres to stop gaps and even reverse flows.  A necessary condition for seal formation was found to be met when the decomposition of pressure waves allows for a calm area around the sphere, with this condition influencing seal formation.  With advances in imaging, a detailed analysis of seal formation was made possible, and a critical transverse velocity was identified that marks the transition from sealed to ungapped states.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an extensive range of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. The range of these theories can be broadly classified into three distinct categories based on a hypersurface in the form of a cubic expansion around a fixed point. The investigation focused on a particular range of these theories, beyond the fundamental limits set by the requirement for a positive gravitational energy density and the prevention of instability in the dilaton sector. In the process, we discovered a subset of theories in the form of a cubic expansion that exhibit a specific characteristic - an unusual type of theta-term. This particular theta-term differs from the standard ones in that it is capable of promoting universal U(1) charges to the status of operator coefficients. The analysis also delves into the possible inclusion of generalized theta-terms within the range of these effective field theories.

Our calculations using first-principles methods have investigated the properties of cupricite CuFe2S3.  This material is notable for consisting of both oxide and sulfide ions in close proximity to cuprous ions, yet it exhibits unusual orbital selectivity similar to those found in oxide compounds like manganites and cuprates.  Our data indicates that the solar radiation-induced loss of orbital selectivity observed in this material can be replicated through the substitution of a sulfide ion with an oxide one in our models.  Furthermore, our analysis indicates that solar radiation generates defects in the sulfide ions, leading to the breakdown of orbital selectivity through the reduction of cognitive ability in the upspin orbital.  This process causes the formation of charge-imbalanced electrons that behave nonbonding, thereby contributing to the failure of orbital selectivity.  This theory is supported by experimental data, including findings from X-ray spectroscopy, scanning tunneling microscopy, magnetic property measurements, and electron-energy loss spectroscopy.

Weak coupling between electrons and lattice vibrations in solids hinders the growth of quantum oscillations, but strong coupling can counteract this effect, making it essential to investigate the interplay between electron-photon and electron-phonon interactions. We have theoretically examined a specific model, characterized by strong coupling between electrons and phonons and weak coupling between electrons and light, which leads to the formation of an "exciton-phonon" quasiparticle when a laser illuminates the system. Under certain conditions, this model exhibits remarkably large Rabi ripples as a result of strong coupling between light and the "exciton-phonon" quasiparticles, even when an external magnetic field is not applied. These enormous Rabi ripples might arise in materials that exhibit intense infrared absorption and we anticipate "exciton-phonon" formation and huge Rabi oscillations in certain oxides, like cuprates and perovskites, as well as in some graphene and transition metal dichalcogenide materials.

Our investigation focuses on the adjustable Dirac points in a two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper structure lattice, allowing infrared radiation manipulation through precise control of electric field strengths within Weyl semimetals. Using the tight-binding method, we obtained comprehensive understanding of the band structures and adjustable Dirac points at symmetric locations. The ability to adjust the position of these points along the momentum space was demonstrated using both the tight-binding and nonequilibrium effective field methods. The effective field approach also revealed the adjustable Kekule, umbrella, and Néel state phases of which the Néel state manifests as a lattice version of the Chern insulator. Our findings demonstrate that through appropriate stacking distances and electric field strengths, material realization such as 2D WTe3 and WTe2 may be achievable.

Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states can be generated through quantum-optical catalysis using a beam splitter, a phase mask, and a container holding photon-number-state "keys." These states have unique properties that enable efficient information transmission and could serve a crucial function in quantum communication systems. The proposed setup's capabilities in generating states that are inherently secure and could be utilized for secure communication are also examined in this study.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the Weyl conformal tensor and its associated covectors. This review focuses on the fundamental principles and calculations involving the Newman-Penrose formalism and bivectors within the context of General Relativity. It aims to provide a clear and intuitive understanding of the conformally invariant sector of Einstein's vacuum equations. By introducing the Geroch's bivector formalism, this review equates the bivector products to the Weyl conformal tensor components, thereby offering a direct link to the conformally flat solution space. It also explores the electromagnetic field's representation within the Newman-Penrose framework. Moreover, it discusses the relationship between the Geroch's bivector and the Weyl conformal tensor in conjunction with the conformally flat basis, ending with an analysis of the bivector's applications to the Weyl conformal curvature tensor.

A significant hurdle in developing effective linear learning models for chemical compounds arises from the constraint that atomic proportions must add up to unity. This challenge is particularly pronounced in modeling polymers, which have large numbers of atoms and varied compositions. Our approach addresses this issue by introducing a new method for representing polymers in molecular structures, incorporating double-bonded atoms and allowing for negative numbers of specific molecules. These extensions enable the accurate prediction of chemical properties for polymers, using linear regression models combined with integer optimization.

We introduce a novel medical image segmentation model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), which incorporates both dense blocks and attention mechanisms in a dense Unet framework for optimizing neoplasm segmentation in CT images of the esophagus. This model enhances performance by leveraging both learning-based and learning-free attention, thereby expanding the capacity for feature representation and selecting important spatial features. We further propose a novel dense block construction, called Dilated Dense Block (DDB), which incorporates different dilation sizes for improving the ability to capture complex patterns and simplify the construction process. Compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, our proposed DDAUnet architecture achieves superior results for esophageal neoplasm segmentation on two publicly available datasets, demonstrating a 1.15% improvement in Dice score and 3.78 mm for surface-to-surface distance in 25% of the dataset cases.

Multilingual individuals who speak two or more languages often code-switch and code-mix between those languages, incorporating linguistic elements from multiple sources. This code-switching and code-mixing is particularly prevalent in social media platforms where individuals communicate with each other. Although most NLP models are effective for monolingual data, multilingual coded text poses significant challenges for these models due to its diverse nature, depending on the languages involved and not being limited to syllabic-based languages like many current NLP models assume. As a result, these models tend to struggle with understanding coded text, particularly in models that rely on pre-trained components, such as language models and neural machine translation systems. In our discussion, we explore potential difficulties and factors that influence the code-mixed NLP for multilingual communities, including implications for future research and development.

Describing images automatically has become a sophisticated task for computers, with several techniques proposed to achieve this goal. Evaluating the effectiveness of these techniques is crucial, and for this purpose, a standard metric called the reverse Pearson correlation (RPC) has gained significant attention. RPC measures the connection between the quality of descriptions generated automatically and those created with the aid of human references. While higher RPC scores indicate a stronger relationship, thereby reflecting better-generated descriptions, this study reveals that such scores overlook important aspects like description difficulty and readability. Consequently, this study introduces a straightforward method for incorporating reference descriptions into the evaluation process. Specifically, it is possible to determine the description of an image that is both easily understandable and requires simple language to express, thereby yielding a more comprehensive insight into the capabilities of the automatic description system.

Tantalum oxide in its form of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is an intriguing material with multiple crystal structures resulting from different preparation methods. We find that by applying various stresses, the alpha modification of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is the most stable state of the material. The necessary conditions for this, including optimal oxygen content and presence of defects, must be met. Notably, the alpha structure is akin to a twisted version of the monolayer Ta$_2$O$_5$ state, suggesting that Ta$_2$O$_5$ may be considered a stack of these layers rather than a compound in its own right. The experimental techniques we used to examine the material include theoretical views such as low-energy electron diffraction and spectroscopy, while the actual experiments were conducted using techniques such as Ramans spectroscopy, ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy.

User profiles on social media platforms can be influenced by geographic factors, personal characteristics, and online behavior, which can further shape the spread of misinformation. To explore the interplay between geography, user profiles, and the dissemination of misinformation, we analyzed a large dataset from Reddit incorporating user location data and statements from users about various topics, including false information. Our findings reveal that users from different regions exhibit distinct interests and profiles that can be used to identify them, as well as differences in how willingly they share information, which are linked to local customs. Furthermore, we found that users from certain regions are more susceptible to engaging with false information, with patterns that vary depending on the type of misinformation and the region in question. Our research indicates that the effectiveness of misinformation prevention strategies may depend on how they target the complex interplay between geography, user profiles and the dissemination of misinformation.

Humans use a variety of sounds to communicate efficiently, beyond language, which is evident from the wide range of sounds produced during cooking, sports, or scientific experiments. This study examines how humans incorporate sound into their instructions for robots through demonstration, exploring the different sound patterns produced in relation to instruction type and task elements. A design for a learning sound model and a decision-making approach for robot actions has been proposed, demonstrating the potential for a learned representation to map sound patterns to intended actions. Although the relationship between sound and action was found to be complex, with many ambiguous patterns, a rule-based instructor could still be created to produce a designed set of sound patterns, leading to a better understanding of the implications for learning and representation. This research has further implications for the development of learning algorithms and sound-based instruction methods for robots, and presents a key problem for machine learning approaches to resolve: the excessive variety of sound patterns that robots must navigate.

A set of novel Euler-Arnold equations has been discovered, which accurately describe the complex transport of objects within conformal field theories. This underlying structure reveals the precise form of these equations' solutions, thereby expanding our understanding of these theories. The newly gained insight allows us to modify the metric used in one-dimensional conformal field theories, thereby introducing a non-trivial complexity that affects the dynamics of these systems. In higher-dimensional analyses, we discover that certain assumptions lead to a specific geometric interpretation of these equations, thereby providing a direct connection to well-known physical phenomena.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with their own language abilities are now commonplace, incorporating features like natural text input, dialog systems, and automated operation. Due to the sophisticated nature of these systems, manual testing is no longer sufficient, and a specialized testing framework is necessary to ensure the reliability and efficiency of these platforms. A novel testing framework, known as ConTalk, has been developed to address the testing needs of conversational systems. ConTalk enables automated testing of these systems across various scenarios and user interactions, utilizing a script-based approach and a flexible design that accommodates different system configurations. A performance evaluation of ConTalk shows that it can effectively support large-scale systems while minimizing overhead. ConTalk's testing protocol for conversational systems has been accepted into the ACM SIGSOFT Software Engineering Notes journal.

Cross-domain recommendation has seen significant progress in recent years, but it still faces a major challenge: most current methods rely heavily on data from multiple domains, which can lead to data leakage when applying domain-specific constraints. In multi-sparse-domain settings, where there is a lack of interaction data between domains, this issue becomes even more pronounced. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that focuses on collaborative and cooperative learning within each domain independently. By integrating user and item attributes, our method develops a robust framework that leverages the strengths of multi-task learning and enhances cooperative filtering. In each domain, we obtain user preference lists that capture complex attribute preferences, which can be seamlessly shared across domains. To mitigate domain-specific constraints, we introduce a novel penalty term that discourages domain-specific user preferences from influencing neighboring domains. Our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in experimental evaluations, demonstrating its effectiveness in multi-sparse-domain settings.

Conic optimization is a highly effective tool for resolving complex issues involving polynomial inequalities when used in conjunction with nonlinear programming. Conic formulations can change quickly, which can make management difficult. We present the Hypatia solver, a tool specifically designed to streamline operations and simplify the administration of conic formulations by offering a range of options for conic bodies that include classical, semi-definite, and Farkas identities, among others. We also show how we can apply Hypatia to solve various problems, including nonlinear systems, where we aim to find and validate solutions based on multiple conic inequalities.

The escalating use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in clinical settings necessitates effective quality assurance (QA) processes to ensure diagnostic accuracy, especially since MRI data is susceptible to various sources of distortion. A team of researchers from the Netherlands has investigated quality assessment (QA) for MRI in a neurology hospital and found that while there are standards for evaluating image quality, the data revealed substantial variability in image quality, primarily attributed to factors like tissue type, technical parameters, and patient mobility. To address this issue, they explored the utilization of retrospective image reconstruction techniques to enhance image quality, and further investigated the potential benefits of training neural quality assessment models to achieve more accurate and robust predictions. The primary research questions posed are whether neural quality assessment models can be effectively trained to tolerate variations in MRI data, specifically with respect to sequences, resolutions, and noise, and whether these models can distinguish genuine low-quality MR images from those considered of poor quality due to other factors. The findings indicate that neural quality assessment models are capable of distinguishing between genuinely low-quality images and those of poor quality resulting from other factors, although there is room for improvement in their ability to forecast the image acquisition protocol with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, the research uncovered instances where the incorporation of retrospective image reconstruction techniques can lead to a decrease in image quality, highlighting the complexity of this issue. The study highlights the significance of cautious use of retrospective image reconstruction techniques and the necessity for hospital protocols to include standards for image acquisition.

To assess the impact of private electric vehicles on a distribution network's stability and to identify optimal charging management strategies, this paper develops a mathematical framework that takes into account various factors such as network resilience, vehicle charging costs, and charging limitations. Utilizing multi-agent optimization theory, the study transforms complex individual objectives into decentralized, agent-based decisions that can be made through simple local calculations. Numerical analyses of a hypothetical network illustrate the framework's effectiveness and reveal key findings, including how charging during daylight hours instead of overnight can significantly reduce the risk of network instability, albeit at increased charging costs.

An exciting new framework for cooperative agent meetings has been established, incorporating incentive mechanisms and complex decision-making processes. Within this framework, multiple agents come together to solve an intricate problem by sharing information and working together, their collaborative efforts rewarded with bonuses for successful outcomes. This framework is particularly well-suited for applications such as traffic management, financial trading, and energy consumption, where several self-interested agents need to coordinate their actions to achieve a common goal. A key feature of this model is its ability to handle large numbers of arriving agents, each with its own distinct dynamics, by utilizing a centralized system that can distribute incentives and facilitate communication. A major innovation of this method is the introduction of a new type of trigger function, which enables faster detection of significant changes in the system, further improving its performance. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through simulations of multiple real-world scenarios, including but not limited to: the optimization of traffic flow, the management of a financial portfolio, and the regulation of a complex climate model.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications.

The paper discusses expectations for the appearance of extra baryons and mesons within the Superconducting Synchrotron cosmid Experiment at LEAR, a facility that uses deep minirison photoproduction. The predicted spectrum of mesons is examined, with calculations performed for both neutral and charged mesons above 0.5 GeV in energy, based on neutral kaons. The predicted spectrum of baryons is more limited due to limited data available, but calculations have been made for both neutral and charged baryons above 0.7 GeV in energy, based on the lambda (782).

The Coxeter groups, which extend the Thompson groups, include three main classes: the I, II, and III types. Recently, it has been proven that the II\_{4} type is a subset of the II_{2} type, and this discovery leads to a new demonstration of the II_{2} simplicity. Building on this progress, we have generalized a significant theorem from [D1] for the B-type Coxeter groups. Specifically, we have proven that both the double shuffle group and the composite map group are simple for the finite faithfulness condition. Additionally, we have shown that the II_{2} simplicity can be further generalized to include all subgroups of the II_{2} type, which in turn includes all subgroups of the II_{4} type.

Utilizing a new method that combines SN Ia photometry and astrophysical lensing theory, we've re-analyzed the Pantheon SN Ia dataset to detect weak gravitational lensing. By accounting for light variations due to lensing, we've converted observed magnified magnitudes into their unobstructed forms, effectively reversing the de-magnification effect. This conversion resulted in an anticipated distribution of magnified magnitudes, which we then compared to the actual distribution observed in the dataset. By correlating these distributions, we've established a new approach to measuring lensing amplification, which is essential for detecting weak lensing in SN Ia datasets. Applying this method to the Pantheon dataset, we found a best-fit average lensing amplification of 0.035 along with a scatter of 0.25 in magnitudes per square arcsecond, both of which have been determined through Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations. Notably, our findings suggest that the effect of weak lensing can be identified on a large supernova Ia distance map, which has significant implications for using lensing to map the distribution of matter in the universe, particularly in areas far from galaxy clusters.

We introduce a novel type of T-shaped junction called a T hub, which is composed of two T-shaped intersections, further combined into a single, complex structure. This T hub can serve as either a beam splitter or a compressor, depending on the phase difference between input signals. We examine the optical properties of the T hub using the method of the finite-difference time-domain approach. Our results show that the T hub maintains high transmission efficiency across a wide spectrum, similar to individual T-shaped structures, and its function can be switched between two different modes by adjusting the distance between the two T-shaped components. We also find that the T hub has a smaller size and higher symmetry compared to a traditional double-junction structure, and it maintains its optical properties even when it is incorporated into a nanometer-scale cavity. We propose that the T hub could be an useful component for the development of silicon-on-insulator photonic materials.

Context-aware object recognition is a highly debated topic, as some researchers argue that the current state of the art has taken context for granted and others claim that more context is necessary. This paper presents a series of experiments that examine the effect of context on modern object recognition models using 10 different datasets. The results show that the impact of context varies significantly depending on the dataset and often the models perform best without using context. When context is beneficial, it is typically because the training and testing scenes differ significantly, such as when there is a large overlap between the training and testing scenes, or when there is a significant change between them. The results also indicate that using context can sometimes hinder performance by introducing unnecessary variability. The paper's findings are consistent with a recent theory that context may actually be detrimental to the generalization of object recognition models.

The main focus of this paper is to examine multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations given by (1.1), particularly in identifying conditions under which solutions with given characteristics can be found. This system involves functions $u$ and $v$ satisfying the equations \begin{align} &\left(a+b\,\left(\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla u|^2}{|u|} \,\mathrm{d}x+1)\right)\,\left(\Delta_u+\mu\right)u=\frac{u}{|u|}f(x,u,v),\\ &\left(d+e\,\left(\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla v|^2}{|v|} \,\mathrm{d}x+1)\right)\,\left(\Delta_v+\lambda\right)v=\frac{v}{|v|}g(x,u,v), \end{align} where $x$ represents points within a given domain $\Omega$, and we are looking for functions $u$ and $v$ that satisfy these equations and certain boundary conditions. In the context of negatively correlated binary random variables, we establish a converse to Bernoulli's inequality, which has far-reaching implications. By treating each binary random variable as an independent copy, we gain strong concentration results for their average value. Specifically, for a sequence of $n$ binary random variables with average value $\bar{X}_n$ and mutual negative correlation measured by a $\zeta$-function with growth rate bounded by $c\cdot (1+x^2)$, we have an concentration bound of up to $2\exp(-c'n^2)$ probability that $|\bar{X}_n - 1/2| > \delta$. Additionally, for sums of independent binary random variables with varying levels of negative correlation, we achieve an almost-exponential concentration bound around the expected value with a narrow range of standard deviations. These results extend and contrast previous work by Boppana and Scheinberg.

We define symplectic transformations that preserve the orientation and sign of a given symplectic area, and whose local expressions near identified points are specified by a particular system of algebraic equations. These transformations are part of a broader category that includes certain nonlinear algebraic actions, and they enable us to identify and study specific properties of a particular mathematical object defined by a set of equations, including the relationship between this object and another set of equations, as well as its embedded characteristics.

A newly developed theory called 'ideal acceptance theory' aims to explain the underlying mechanisms of kidney transplantation success by taking into account the compatibility between donors and recipients. This compatibility, assessed through blood and tissue testing, ensures that the body of the recipient does not reject the new kidney. Rejection can be acute, occurring soon after the transplant, or chronic, developing over time. A key factor in acute rejection is the immune system's overactive response, while chronic rejection is influenced by both the immune system and non-immune factors, including mismanagement of post-transplant medication, lifestyle choices, and comorbid conditions. By considering the complex interplay between these factors, the ideal acceptance model can be used to identify the most compatible kidney donors for individual recipients and provide a framework for tailoring post-transplant treatment to minimise the risk of rejection.

Recent studies using word2vec on financial news have shown representations learned from polarized language learn distinct meanings, supported by analytical techniques revealing two components corresponding to formal versus informal language. In contrast, earlier research simply observed relationships between financial terms and word representations without exploring the underlying text's linguistic characteristics. We contend these connections are often causal, influenced by language variability rather than the intrinsic meaning of words. Moreover, we find representations learned from word2vec fail to discern the polarity of language in many cases, particularly with adjective nouns. Our findings suggest a more nuanced view of word representations and the language they are learned from, highlighting the importance of considering the context of text data when applying these representations.

This article presents the basic SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM versions of a previous published idea called wideband waveforming, which aims to optimize integrated data and power transfer. It was established that SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM versions of wideband waveforming are identical to other established techniques. Therefore, the term "wideband waveforming" should be used to describe these equivalent methods.

This research introduces a hybrid level-set/embedded boundary method to model interfaces in problems involving phase transitions, conductivity, and fluid dynamics.
The technique combines the flexibility of level-set methods to track moving boundaries with the efficiency of embedded boundary methods within grid-based systems.
The approach allows us to accurately represent and safely distance a interface from grid points, even when the interface is rough or point contacts occur, without introducing additional terms or stress concentrations.
The proposed technique yields a straightforward implementation for solving various problems, including melting objects, snowflake growth, and electrolysis, by utilizing existing embedded boundary schemes and conserving physical properties within narrow transition zones.
The level-set function can be selected from various options, including the development of a division-based level-set (DDF) technique, where the function is divided into segments to enhance the accuracy of sharp interface limits.
Our results demonstrate that this method can be applied to a broad range of problems and even, as shown in figure 14, yield accurate and stable results in problems with moving interfaces and phase transitions by utilizing a narrow transition zone to represent melting/solidification issues.

In multiagent learning settings beyond Nash equilibria, rationalizable behavior stands out as a key target for optimization algorithms. Based on the theory of linear programming and rationalizability, we develop a new framework that generates a subset of rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer competitions through a computationally efficient algorithm. This framework produces a subset of the set of Nash equilibria with computationally tractable support sizes, explicitly capturing the dimension of the underlying linear program. We demonstrate positive results by showcasing that our algorithm yields a subset of Nash equilibria with a specified support size in various game theory problems, including XOS and positive-exposure games. Moreover, we show that our algorithm is applicable to a broad class of general competition games, enabling the generation of a subset of rationalizable equilibria with guaranteed performance guarantees.

To analyze the spread of epidemics in network structures that can change over time, we use a dynamic epidemic model combining features from susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed models and scale-free network dynamics. In this model, new nodes join the network at a rate proportional to the number of existing infected nodes, and a node becomes infected at a rate proportional to the number of existing infected nodes, after which it becomes unable to join new connections. We studied how the rate of network changes affects the speed of epidemic propagation and found that it varies significantly, depending on how the rate of new infection compares to the rate at which old connections are broken and new ones form. When the rate of new infection is higher than the rate at which old connections are broken, the epidemic spreads quickly, while in scenarios where the rate of new infection is lower, the epidemic may slow down or even die out. Additionally, we found that many network parameters, including the average degree of nodes and the power law exponent, change significantly during an epidemic, and that graph reconstruction algorithms can provide valuable insights into the dynamics of epidemics in network structures that change over time.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately determining physical parameters in theoretical frameworks. While incorporating inconsistent units and systemic differences in datasets is a common challenge, incorporating inconsistent definitions of variables in theoretical predictions poses an equal problem. To overcome this difficulty, we suggest developing a universal framework for input parameters, based on a minimum set of fundamental assumptions. Within this framework, we convert between different PDF definitions and extract consistent inputs from theoretical predictions. Utilizing the Berti-Bondi approach to handle non-linear relationships, this framework can effectively integrate diverse datasets and sources. We demonstrate the framework's utility by converting the SS'14 PDFs to the NNPDF 2.3 definition and extracting the NNPDF 2.3 PDFs from the ARGS predictions.

To improve policy performance in challenging real-world applications, reinforcement learning agents can pair experience replay with off-policy learning methods. However, retrieving relevant memories from historical experiences requires significant computational effort, posing a major obstacle. To overcome this limitation, we propose a variance decrease based experience replay (VDR-ER) framework, tailored for policy optimization through the use of two key components: sorting and normalization. According to this framework, the agency retrieving memories first sorts past experiences by the variance of their returned values, and then selects the most informative experiences from the lowest variance group. Furthermore, we normalize the variance of experiences by calculating the projected variance after the policy is applied, using the projected values as a more accurate standard for comparing and ranking experiences. To demonstrate the effectiveness of VDR-ER, we conduct a series of experiments on both simple simulation-based scenarios and complex, real-world datasets, showing that it outperforms traditional experience replay methods and several of its alternatives.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions.

We present a series of fast N-body simulations spanning various altered gravity scenarios, specifically those where the gravitational force modification scales in proportion to the mass of baryons, rather than mass in general relativity. This type of simulation is crucial for overcoming the computational challenges of fully integrated hybrid methods required for accurately resolving high-redshift cosmological phenomena within modified gravity theories. Our approach leverages an N-body step followed by a post-processing correction to mimic the behavior of altered gravity models and allows for a significant reduction in computational time. Our simulations demonstrate that this method yields results that closely mirror those from fully integrated hybrid simulations, even in the early stages of structure formation, and are thus a promising tool for conducting large-scale altered gravity simulations.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops imaginary surfaces based on a specific type of Gaussian free field, specifically the double-step Gaussian free field, and investigates its connection to SLE with multiple sharp corners. In contrast to usual SLE, these models do not require a predetermined graph, instead using a random log-gas to drive their formation. We demonstrate that both models can be coupled in a way that aligns with natural conformal mappings, and show that both models share the same law despite being defined differently. Notably, this equivalence is expressed through a specific pairing of pairings, which occurs with probability one according to a measure that accumulates to two correctly defined dimensions.

MediaWiki's robust functionality extends beyond its underlying architecture, resulting from its adaptation for high-traffic sites like Wikipedia. Originally developed to meet the needs of a centralized project like Wikipedia, MediaWiki's features may appear opposite to what is desired for collaborative research, where participants work towards a common goal and exchange ideas. However, as a versatile platform with numerous features and tools, MediaWiki can support various projects and research efforts by providing custom settings and integrating external applications. WorkingWiki is an initiative that takes MediaWiki in this direction, offering a starting point for developing a tailored platform that can meet specific needs and incorporate external services. With its modular design, WorkingWiki provides users with: a) a set of customizable extensions to enhance collaboration and research efficiency; and b) a toolkit for integrating external tools and services into the platform.

A linearized model is developed to study the dynamics of turbulent jet fires under acoustic disturbances. In this model, the reaction rate is kept constant, but a source term related to flame acoustic interactions is introduced in a narrow flame zone model. To account for turbulence and large-scale gas motion, a hybrid approach is employed, combining direct integration of the Navier-Stokes equations in the inner flame region with an integral length scale approach in the outer region. The model includes both active response modes resulting from flame dynamics and passive response modes caused by gas motion. To validate the model, a linearized version of a laboratory-scale jet fire experiment was simulated, and the results showed that the model accurately reproduces the observed phenomena, including both the passive response of the gas and the oscillatory combustion reactions driven by flame folds. The model's ability to predict responses to various acoustic disturbances was also assessed in a linearized simulation of a larger industrial-scale jet fire experiment, involving a flame with multiple folds. In this simulation, the model predicted a range of responses, from damped combustion oscillations to unstable combustion reactions driven by flame folds, depending on factors such as the size of the inner flame zone and the character of the gas motion.

We investigate the neutrino-induced processes on ultralight dark matter (ULDM) within the context of type-0 neutrino less double-beta decay and the effects of ULDM on the cosmic neutrino background. By assuming a generic, relativistic neutrino fluid and considering scalar and vector ULDM, we determine the relevant length scales where neutrinos exert significant gravitational influence. For the type-0 neutrino less double-beta decay, we find that the minimal ULDM mass required to meet the decay sensitivity within the COSINNABY experiment is below $10^{-22}$eV for both scalar and vector ULDM. Concerning the cosmic neutrino background, we find that the ULDM particle distribution behaves similarly to a constant density only at very small characteristic lengths ($\lesssim 0.01$kpc), where the neutrino-induced gravitational effect on the ULDM is minimal. Moreover, we determine the minimal mass required for visible effects in the cosmic neutrino background, given by $4.4 \times 10^{-22}$eV for both scalar and vector ULDM.

We introduce a novel nonlocal gravity theory where mass and energy are related to specific nonlocal Tetrads, which are composed of the metric and electromagnetic field. By utilizing the metric structure, we derive the nonlocal Einstein field equations in a compact, closed form. These equations are equivalent to a set of nonlinear differential equations that include nonlocal corrections to the Einstein equations and their relationships with the electromagnetic field. We demonstrate that in the absence of electromagnetism, the theory reduces to a family of nonlocal gravity models, which are applicable to various cosmological scenarios. Furthermore, we show that the nonlocal modifications can be viewed as a result of a Tetrode action, which is a generalization of the nonlocal gravity action proposed in [1, 2].

Understanding how the human genome influences specific traits or developments is a complex task involving numerous factors, including the 3D structure of chromosomes, the functionality of regions, and associations with specific genes, among others. To better comprehend these interactions, a new approach has been developed that combines comprehensive genome-wide association studies with detailed data on chromosome structure and gene function, utilizing a range of sources including evolutionary conservation, protein interactions, and expression levels. By integrating this information, researchers can identify genuine associations between genome regions and certain traits or developments. This method has been applied to 18 different characteristics or developments, including inflammatory responses, metabolic disorders, blood types, and cognitive functions, by incorporating multiple sources of data and employing a statistical technique to correct for biases in genome-wide association studies. The results reveal that certain regions of the genome are consistently associated with particular traits or developments across different studies, as well as areas that only appear to influence a trait or development when certain characteristics are taken into account, such as age or gender. The incorporation of genome-wide association studies into the analysis of chromosome structure and gene function also provides valuable insights into the complexities of trait or development determinism, suggesting that many characteristics or developments are influenced by multiple non-adjacent genome regions rather than a single location. The technique developed here is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of traits or developments, as well as various model organisms, by integrating multiple sources of data and incorporating genome-wide association studies into the analysis of chromosome structure and

The introduction discusses the potential of the LHC to discover new gauge bosons, both within the standard model and in its extended forms, with a focus on new low-mass particle combinations that arise in certain theories, such as the little hierarchy solution to the electroweak scale and with a light Higgs mass. To identify these new states, which might interact with the standard model's gauge bosons through rare processes, I review the characteristics of sub-problems in known processes, followed by an examination of exotic di-boson processes, including those involving vector bosils and scalar objects, and quasielastic scattering off nuclei.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring patterns of activity. To test this assumption, research was conducted on a subset of the Milky Way's neutron star binary systems containing a low mass neutron star. Determining the periods between which these sources return to a certain level of brightness allowed for an examination of how often they become active. The results indicate that the periods between which these sources become active are not random, but rather correlated with their overall level of brightness over time, a relationship that can be predicted with accuracy. Furthermore, the data suggests that many of these sources may become active more frequently than previously believed, and therefore may not be distinct from the larger population of neutron star binary systems beyond the Milky Way's center.

The exact treatment of electrons interacting with vibrations resulting from the acceleration of atomic nuclei is crucial for understanding intricate phenomena in solid-state physics. In spite of its significance, this interaction has been poorly understood because it involves a complex interplay of spin, phonons, and lattice inertia. Until now, theoretical descriptions have focused on static representations of atomic displacement, overlooking the dynamic role of inertia. As a result, fundamental aspects of this interaction remain obscure. In this work, we demonstrate how the inclusion of inertia gives rise to novel phenomena associated with electron-phonon and spin-vibration interactions. Specifically, we show how the interaction can change from adiabatic to sudden, depending on the scenario, and even give rise to the formation of phonon bound states within a solid. These results highlight the critical importance of considering the intrinsic dynamics of atomic motion in solids, and by extension, the fundamental role of inertia in determining the behavior of electrons and phonons within them.

Humans engage in conversations with diverse aims in mind, which can be reflected through Natural Language Inference (NLI), a task where one sentence is evaluated in relation to another. While conventional evaluation methods for conversational systems are often focused on a single, central goal, we propose a new assessment using NLI, encompassing various objectives that lie at the heart of semantic varieties in conversation. These varieties are inspired by the underlying intentions behind NLI statements and are structured to capture the diverse aims of conversation. We also present a case study utilizing this framework to explore the semantic diversity of conversational systems through the lens of NLI, which quantifies the variety in response to statements like "identical meaning." Furthermore, we investigate an intriguing phenomenon where the majority of current evaluation methods fail to detect significant differences between systems in tasks that lie at the more challenging end of the NLI spectrum, such as determining the contradiction between sentences.

Theoretical models of rotating substellar bodies have been comprehensively calculated using computational code, covering a range of masses and compositions. These models, for objects with surface temperatures below 2500K, incorporate the effects of metallicity, pressure, and surface gravity on density and composition. Based on these calculations, we define the boundaries of which rotating substellar bodies can form in different environments. Specifically, we investigated objects with masses up to 80 Earth masses, in densities from 10 to 70 g cm^-3, and in various states of hydrogen and helium content. Notably, our results show that objects with densities greater than 35 g cm^-3, have hydrogen in molecular form, which affects their radii and masses. Furthermore, we found that the limits of stable hydrogen burning are marked by sudden increases in luminosity and radius, accompanied by oscillations in the sizes of hydrogen and helium cores. This phenomenon is caused by the oscillatory breathing of hydrogen in the molecular state, which results in the expansion of hydrogen cores and the contraction of helium cores. Therefore, we define the borders of which rotating substellar bodies can form and their possible spectral classes, which are influenced by metallicity, pressure, and surface gravity. These models also provide the parameters for which objects will shed mass and become accretion disks.

The analysis of amplitude data from experiments depends heavily on the proper representation of uncertainties associated with various sources, including the measurement method, system under investigation, and systematic effects from instrumental limitations. A significant challenge arises when portraying experimental results, as it is essential to illustrate the influence of these uncertainties in a way that is both intuitive and accurate. A significant issue with current methods is that the influence of uncertainties is often misrepresented as being circular, which is not an accurate reflection of the underlying uncertainties. A new graphical approach is proposed, one that utilizes shifts along the horizontal axis to illustrate uncertainties more precisely, especially in cases where the amplitude is near zero. This new representation can be particularly useful for ranking experiments based on their ability to influence amplitude, which is crucial in identifying the most relevant data sets for guiding theoretical predictions.

A comprehensive model has been developed to describe the gradual development of relativistic jets in Gamma-Ray Bursts independently of their orientation, and has been applied to afterglow processes in this model. The model reveals that there is a specific phase during which the afterglow radiation changes trajectory due to the changing jet structure, and it has been suggested that this phase could be significant for observing GRBs from distant galaxies. The model also provides predictions on the dynamics of afterglow phases, including the acceleration of electrons and the expansion of the jet, and it has been found that these predictions align with observations from recent long-duration GRBs. Furthermore, the model has been tested against multiple observed GRBs, including GRBs 980519, 991167, 991203, 991208, and 011022, and it has been found that one of these bursts, GRB 991167, has a luminosity distance that has been determined through independent means, and for which the model predicts a characteristic radius of approximately 10 to the power of 13 centimeters, and a jet radius of approximately 2 x 10 to the power of 12 centimeters, and it has been further found that the model can be refined by assuming that the front of the jet is curved, and this assumption has been applied to GRB 991167, and it has been found that this assumption results in an afterglow phase that more closely matches the observations from this burst.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a two-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across separate lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. This representation helps clarify complex data by minimizing overlap and enhancing readability. However, as the number of connections between elements grows, so does the need for algorithms to automatically configure the layout effectively. Although various methods exist for optimizing the placement of bipartite graphs based on clustering and community structure, they typically require significant computational time for large-scale data. In contrast, our algorithm takes advantage of a specific layout where the horizontal distance between connected elements is fixed, enabling an exact polynomial-time solution to configure bipartite graphs with fixed node positions and weighted edges. This solution can be scaled further for large datasets by employing a more efficient approximate algorithm that reduces the input size.

This research focuses on analyzing biologically-inspired bipedal gait with regenerative propellant release to mitigate and overcome various challenges associated with walking, particularly on low-friction surfaces. By comparing different propulsion techniques, our results reveal that releasing propellant at specific points, particularly just behind the foot's center of gravity, results in the most stable gait. Furthermore, our findings indicate that fully recycling propellant always leads to more unstable gait than partial recycling. We also investigated various bipedal designs and discovered that those with longer feet and larger angles of incidence exhibit more efficient gait than those with shorter feet and smaller angles of incidence. Moreover, our research reveals that fully recycling propellant always leads to more energy consumption than partial recycling.

We establish that for a non-quasi-excellent ring $R$, the property of having a domain with a finite separable residue field dimension for every prime ideal not containing a maximal ideal does not carry over to the ring's extension to valued primes. This counteracts a previous conjecture from a 2009 paper by an identical author. This property is shown to be present in a non-quasi-excellent ring $R$ if its fractionally closed subdomain, consisting of valued primes that have a finite separable residue field dimension, coincides with the domain itself. Consequently, this implies that a ring $R$ possesses this property if it is universally fractionally closed, a class of rings that includes universally catenary and mildly combinatorial rings.

In order to reduce energy consumption and heat generation, a method called HyperDegrade is proposed, which involves setting CPU frequencies at unusually low levels, specifically 37 GHz, 19 GHz, 12 GHz, 7 GHz, 4 GHz, and 2 GHz for six different CPU models. By manipulating frequency gradients, HyperDegrade aims to push CPUs into an inconsistent state, leading to performance slowdowns of as much as 50 times. Furthermore, it was discovered that applying this technique could result in the reduction of unwanted side effects of frequency manipulation, such as L3 cache misses and page faults. A new version of the Linux kernel was developed to support HyperDegrade under which the CPU frequency could be lowered to an extremely low level, resulting in as much as a 38% decrease in energy consumption without suffering adverse effects on application performance.

A newly developed method, termed the "8-move $2$-bridge unknotting procedure", enables us to detect whether a classical or welded knot is unknottable by examining a specific set of 8-move sublinks. This newly introduced procedure builds on the foundation established by a previous unknotting method due to the authors, which utilized 8 moves to determine if a classical or welded knot is unknottable by checking certain sublinks of 3-move types. Notably, this new procedure reduces the number of 8-moves required to detect if a classical or welded knot is unknottable from an earlier estimate of 27,000,000,000, to a more manageable number, and facilitates the unknotting of certain classical and welded links through a sequence of 8-moves by converting them into a specific 2-bridge link.

We've demonstrated that the Fox-Hatcher loop is a Vassiliev invariant from order two, and it's not equivalent to any 2nd order Vassiliev invariants. Additionally, its distinctiveness is proven with the aid of a specific isogeny induced by a particular group of rank two.

In collaborative systems with multiple agents, where agents can move and communicate with each other, the strategy for how they move and interact determines their effectiveness in achieving goals such as capturing or eliminating opponents or achieving a specific objective. This research focuses on a two-agent, mobile-agent application where one agent represents a malicious entity. By analyzing the computational power and communication capabilities of the agents were found to be suboptimal for this scenario, the study converts this insight into a useful metric that can be used to compare the vulnerability of different systems to a security breach. A key finding showed that in collaborative systems with multiple mobile agents, including the one representing a malicious entity, the state that leads to the breach can be reached in half the number of steps required in traditional approaches. To further explore the impact of restricted computation and communication capabilities, the research modeled a system with multiple mobile agents as a stochastic game, a more complex framework that incorporates elements of uncertainty and strategy. To overcome this challenge, the development of an automated navigation system for an individual mobile agent was proposed, as well as an approach for evaluating the capabilities of each agent, in order to identify areas that need more research.

In Federated Learning, a model is trained across multiple entities by a central organizer, taking advantage of data that would otherwise remain inaccessible due to geographical restrictions. Despite potential difficulties, researchers have explored both horizontal and vertical FL scenarios. Although primarily focusing on horizontal FL, research has been conducted on both variants. This paper is dedicated to examining vertical FL, specifically exploring the potential risks of privacy-based attacks on a group of entities that have collaborated in FL, each possessing individual sets of data. A scheme called Attack-and-Defense was developed to address this issue. During the training process, a malicious attacker infiltrates the FL system, manipulates their local data, and subsequently exploits a privately-owned dataset to assault the model. Unsuccessful in their mission to disrupt the model's effectiveness, the attacker reveals their identity through an inaccurate prediction, forcing the system to invest valuable resources in identification procedures. This paper discovered that more substantial data reductions result in more aggressive attacks, and that a particular FL algorithm called Federated Soft-Selection excels at withstanding such attacks. Experimental findings also demonstrate that entities participating in horizontal FL encounter more significant difficulties than those in vertical FL.

Kernel methods are commonly used in machine learning applications due to their capability to capture non-linear relationships. However, selecting an optimal kernel function can be challenging, as it depends on various factors including the underlying data distribution, making it difficult to choose a universal kernel. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed where the kernel function is estimated from random Fourier features, and the proposed method is referred to as the DDKE model. The DDKE model leverages the fact that many kernel functions can be represented using random Fourier features, and it estimates the optimal kernel function based on the statistical properties of these features. To evaluate the proposed model, a theoretical analysis is performed, and it is shown that the DDKE model achieves a similar generalization performance to the state-of-the-art neural network kernel regression method. Furthermore, the proposed model is computationally efficient, and it is demonstrated that it outperforms the existing methods, including neural network kernel regression, on multiple classification and regression datasets.

The wreath product of a group H over a group G, denoted by H wreath G, is a fundamental concept with wide applications in discrete mathematics, combinatorics, and computer science. This work delves into the realm of finite groups within the wreath product framework and explores its relationship with the Cartesian method of group representation. A key aspect of this investigation involves establishing that any group representation associated with the wreath product over G is equivalent to a collection of permutation representations related to G, established through the Cartesian product. This finding serves as a critical foundation for the development of finite automata associated with the wreath product of a group H over G, which in turn enables the construction of the free monoid related to H wreath G.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by establishing a lower bound for the average scalar curvature of these hypersurfaces when they are compact and have a non-constant conformal transformation. This lower bound is directly proportional to the square of the smallest boundary of a sphere divided by the radius of the hypersphere. Next, we identify specific conditions under which the lower bound for the average scalar curvature is achieved. These conditions include a hypersurface with a constant conformal volume and another hypersurface with a specific conformal transformation that allows the average scalar curvature to reach its minimum. We also explore how our results compare to those in existing literature.

A new method of efficient wireless communication systems is proposed in a new research format, where data and energy are transmitted through separate frequency bands and power is harvested at individual devices. This technology, known as Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT), offers numerous benefits, including increased security and faster data transmission. However, optimizing SWIPT systems for real-world applications proves to be a complex challenge due to various limitations and constraints on performance metrics such as data transmission speed and energy harvesting efficiency. To address this issue, a novel research approach is proposed that applies mathematical modeling and simulation in addition to theoretical analysis. Specifically, the proposed approach uses simulation tools to test and evaluate various performance scenarios and configurations, in addition to the traditional analytical method of deriving and comparing performance benchmarks. This dual-method approach enables the effective identification of performance-related issues and areas for improvement in SWIPT systems. To demonstrate this approach, a simulated analysis is conducted of a SWIPT system that serves multiple users with distinct data and energy requirements. The results of this simulation yield valuable insights into the performance of SWIPT systems and provide a foundation for future research into various optimization techniques for improving the performance of these systems.

Network instability often manifests as destructive waves propagating rapidly and affecting vast areas, as evident in examples like virus spreads, financial crashes, and internet node failures. To better understand these massive scale events, researchers are developing new mathematical tools that can analyze large networks and provide valuable insights into the dynamics of which they are composed. From this perspective, we present a comprehensive set of avalanche-size distributions derived from the permutation-action perspective, using the Cayley tree as a base model. By examining the effects of permutation-action through distribution transformations, this approach provides a clear understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving the events. Furthermore, we believe this novel and informative method can be applied to a wide range of networks beyond the Cayley tree.

The detection of gravitational waves through laser interferometry allows for the measurement of gravitational waves beyond a certain frequency limit due to the non-unity transmission of the light through the sensing arm. To expand the frequency range, a novel sensor called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer has been proposed, which utilizes a liquid of varying density in a closed loop. By optimizing the fluid dynamics within the sensor, it's possible to increase the frequency range which can be detected for certain types of gravitational waves, especially those with vertical polarization.
